This is a SECOND FOLLOW-UP literature query for an undergraduate-mentored
research demonstration. The first Edison LITERATURE_HIGH task on this topic
(1b90208d-3555-4479-9db0-512d67e69f5f) covered egg fracture mechanics,
tensegrity topology selection, and instrumentation for a drop test of a raw
chicken egg on a multi-material 3D-printed (PETG strut + TPU 85A tendon)
tensegrity. The first follow-up (f41b7034-439e-45de-b97f-4bf1d85b9811)
proposed an apples-to-apples drag-free egg-drop benchmark with shared
constraints (Ø 200 mm bounding sphere, m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg ≈ 55 g, ASTM

/ η_V / N_reuse). Please do NOT re-derive that material — focus only on the
new question below.

NEW QUESTION (from the project lead):

Keith A. Brown's lab at Boston University (PI: Prof. Keith A. Brown,
Mechanical Engineering / Materials Science, BU) has published a series of
papers on "superlative" or "record-setting" mechanical energy absorbing
structures discovered using autonomous / Bayesian-optimization closed-loop
experimentation — the BEAR ("Bayesian Experimental Autonomous Researcher")
self-driving lab and successor systems. Representative references include:

  - Gongora, Snapp, Whiting, et al., "A Bayesian experimental autonomous
    researcher for mechanical design," Science Advances 6, eaaz1708 (2020).
  - Snapp et al. and follow-on BEAR / autonomous-design papers from the
    Brown group on FFF-printed energy-absorbing structures.
  - Any subsequent "superlative" / "record-setting" energy-absorption
    structure papers from this group (please surface the most recent and
    most-cited follow-ups, including any review articles).

Please answer all of the following, with peer-reviewed citations:

1. **What exactly did Brown's group report?**
   Summarize the 2–4 most relevant Brown-lab publications on
   energy-absorbing structures: what was the design space (parametric
   FFF-printed lattice / hollow-strut / unit-cell family?), what was the
   loading mode (quasi-static uniaxial compression? drop-tower impact?
   strain rate?), what was the reported figure of merit (toughness J/cm³,
   SEA J/g, plateau stress, energy ratio η = E_abs / (σ_max · ε)?), and
   what numerical record(s) did they claim relative to prior art?
   List the geometry families they explored (e.g. concave hexagonal
   honeycombs, beam-tied unit cells, BO-discovered topologies, etc.).

2. **Loading-regime applicability to a drag-free egg drop.**
   Were Brown's "superlative" results obtained under (a) quasi-static
   compression (mm/min), (b) low-velocity impact (drop-tower at <5 m/s),
   or (c) high-velocity impact (>10 m/s, free-fall ≥ ~5 m)? Quote the
   reported strain rates / impact velocities. Critically assess whether
   the FoM they report (typically toughness or SEA in quasi-static
   compression) extrapolates to peak-deceleration / survival in a free-
   fall egg drop. Specifically, does the BEAR ranking of geometries
   change between quasi-static crush and impact (any published evidence,
   or any general result from the cellular-solids / metamaterials
   literature relating quasi-static SEA to impact peak-g or h_crit)?

3. **Single-use vs reusable.**
   Are the Brown-lab structures single-use (densified and destroyed during
   the energy-absorption event) or reusable (elastic / hyperelastic
   recovery, like a tensegrity)? What polymer / material did the BEAR work
   use (PLA? TPU? other)? How does this map to the categories defined in
   the prior follow-up task (a) crushable foam / lattice cushion,
   (b) elastic recoverable cushion, (e) tensegrity?

4. **Could the Brown-lab "superlative" geometry serve as the upper-bound
   baseline in our benchmark?**
   Under the shared constraints from Edison task f41b7034 (Ø 200 mm
   bounding sphere, m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg ≈ 55 g, rigid concrete floor
   per ASTM D5276, h up to 15 m), would it be defensible to:
   (i) FFF-print the BEAR-discovered "best" unit cell as a solid cushion
       block (or cell tessellation) of the same bounding volume,
   (ii) use it as a *baseline* curve on the recommended demo plot
       (peak g vs drop height with the egg-fracture survivability band),
   (iii) interpret it as the **closed-loop-optimized baseline** representing
       what an automated BO search converges to within a parametric
       design space, against which the tensegrity (which is a
       *topologically distinct* class-1 cable-strut shell, not in the
       BEAR search space) is compared?
   Please give an explicit yes / no / yes-with-caveats recommendation,
   and identify any technical issues:
       - Can the BEAR optimal cell be re-printed faithfully on a
         consumer FFF printer (Bambu H2D class) given that BEAR papers
         report the optimal geometry parameters?
       - Is the BEAR FoM (quasi-static toughness J/cm³) at all
         comparable to peak-g in a free-fall drop, or is the comparison
         apples-to-oranges?
       - Are there licensing / reproducibility constraints (proprietary
         BO model, unreleased optimal-geometry STL)?
       - Does the "superlative" claim hold under impact loading, or
         only under quasi-static loading?

5. **Better alternative baselines if BEAR is not appropriate.**
   If the BEAR / Brown-lab geometry is *not* a fair baseline for a
   drag-free egg drop (because of loading-regime mismatch or
   non-reproducibility), what would be the closest defensible "BO-optimized
   FFF-printed energy absorber" baseline from the autonomous-design or
   metamaterials literature that *is* reported under impact loading?
   Examples to consider: Gu et al. (MIT, BO-optimized composites under
   drop-tower impact); the autonomous-design literature on auxetic /
   hierarchical lattices under impact; any recent follow-on work
   (2023–2026) extending BEAR-style autonomous design to impact regimes.

6. **Concrete recommendation.**
   In one paragraph, recommend either (a) include a Brown-lab BEAR-derived
   FFF lattice as the **"BO-optimized lattice baseline"** alongside the
   foam, honeycomb, and tensegrity entries on the demo plot, OR
   (b) decline to use BEAR as a baseline and instead cite it as
   conceptually-related prior art for *how to discover* the optimal
   tensegrity (i.e., apply the BEAR methodology to our class-1 tensegrity
   design space), explaining the reasoning either way. Note that the
   project itself is a Bayesian-optimization-of-tensegrities effort, so
   the framing "BEAR for tensegrities" is the natural narrative if the
   geometry is not directly comparable.

Please cite specific peer-reviewed papers, conference proceedings, and
technical reports where applicable. Quantitative claims should include
units and a primary source.

# Assessment of Brown-Lab BEAR Energy-Absorbing Structures as a Baseline for a Tensegrity Egg-Drop Benchmark

## 1. What Exactly Did Brown's Group Report?

Brown's group at Boston University has published a progression of three core papers on autonomous discovery of energy-absorbing structures, culminating in a record-setting result.

**Gongora et al. (2020), *Science Advances*.** The inaugural BEAR paper explored a parametric "crossed barrel" geometry family defined by a 4-dimensional design vector (n, θ, r, t) — number of hollow columns, twist angle, outer radius, and wall thickness — connecting two circular platforms (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3). Structures were FFF-printed in PLA on MakerGear M3 desktop printers and tested under uniaxial quasi-static compression at 3 mm/min on an Instron 5965 with a 4.8 kN force limit (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6). The figure of merit was toughness U (area under the force–displacement curve, in joules). A grid search of 600 designs found toughness spanning 0.3–51.5 J (mean 15.3 J), and the BO-guided BEAR identified the optimal design tuple (12, 131°, 1.95 mm, 1.4 mm) with approximately a 60-fold reduction in experiments relative to grid search (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6).

**Gongora et al. (2021), *iScience*.** This follow-up coupled the same crossed-barrel family with finite element analysis (FEA)-informed transfer learning, where an FEA-predicted resilience surrogate served as a Bayesian prior and a discrepancy model was learned via Gaussian process regression (gongora2021usingsimulationto pages 4-6). Importantly, the authors noted that toughness (the plastic deformation–dominated quantity relevant to energy absorption) was not reliably predicted by FEA because of the difficulty of modeling self-contact and plasticity, and that toughness and simulated resilience were uncorrelated (gongora2021usingsimulationto pages 4-6). Loading was again quasi-static compression of PLA components (gongora2021usingsimulationto pages 2-4).

**Gongora et al. (2022), *Matter*.** A paper titled "Designing lattices for impact protection using transfer learning" was identified in search results but the full text was not retrievable for this review. Its title indicates that this may be the first Brown-lab work to extend the BEAR framework toward impact-loading contexts.

**Snapp et al. (2024), *Nature Communications*.** The flagship "superlative" paper expanded the design space to a generalized cylindrical shell (GCS) family defined by 11 geometric parameters — diameter, height, wall thickness, plus eight cross-section perturbation parameters (x₁–x₈) controlling lobed profiles and twist — yielding effectively trillions of unique designs (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 13-16). The human–SDL campaign conducted >25,000 physical experiments across seven polymers and five FFF printers (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 1-4). The figure of merit was energy-absorbing efficiency K_s, a non-dimensional metric defined as the energy absorbed below a threshold stress σ_t relative to the theoretical maximum, with K_s* denoting the peak efficiency at optimal σ_t* (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 2-3, snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2). The campaign discovered a record-setting structure with K_s = 75.2%, surpassing the prior synthetic record (plastic foam, K_s = 68.1%) and the natural best (balsa wood, K_s = 71.8%) (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 16-20). The best-performing PLA design "Willow" achieved K_s* = 73.3 ± 0.9%, while the best TPU-2 design "Iroko" achieved K_s* = 53 ± 4% (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10). SHAP analysis attributed ~90% of the performance improvement to four-lobed profile and twist parameters (x₂–x₃, x₆–x₈), with high performers concentrating around relative density ρ_r ≈ 0.1 and d/t ≈ 20 (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10).

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gongora 2020, *Science Advances* | Parametric crossed-barrel structures; 4D space \((n, \theta, r, t)\) generated from OpenSCAD/STL workflow (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6) | Uniaxial quasi-static compression on Instron 5965 at **3 mm/min**; no impact loading reported (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6) | Toughness **U** = area under force-displacement curve, in **J** (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6) | Grid search over 600 designs found toughness spanning **0.3–51.5 J**; best design reported as “(12, 131°, 1.95 mm, 1.4 mm)” (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 2-3, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6) | PLA on FDM/FFF printers (gongora2021usingsimulationto pages 2-4, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 4-5) | Effectively **single-use / crushable** under the reported high-strain compression paradigm; no elastic-recovery result emphasized (gongora2021usingsimulationto pages 2-4, gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6) |

*Table: This table summarizes the most relevant Brown-lab BEAR publications for mechanical energy absorption, emphasizing geometry family, loading regime, figure of merit, best reported performance, materials, and whether the structures behave as crushable or recoverable absorbers.*

## 2. Loading-Regime Applicability to a Drag-Free Egg Drop

**All published BEAR results were obtained under quasi-static compression.** The original 2020 study used 3 mm/min displacement on an Instron (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6), and the 2024 campaign used 2 mm/min (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 13-16). For the sample heights tested (~20 mm), this corresponds to nominal strain rates of order 10⁻³ s⁻¹ — firmly in the quasi-static regime. No impact testing (drop-tower or otherwise) was reported in the retrievable papers, with the possible exception of the 2022 *Matter* paper whose full content was unavailable.

**Extrapolation to free-fall egg-drop impact is problematic.** A drag-free egg drop from, say, 5 m produces an impact velocity of approximately 10 m/s (ε̇ on the order of 10²–10³ s⁻¹ for a 20 mm cushion), representing a strain-rate increase of five to six orders of magnitude over the BEAR test conditions. The cellular-solids literature demonstrates that geometry rankings under quasi-static loading do not necessarily hold under dynamic impact. Zhao et al. (2005) showed that different cellular geometries exhibit markedly different rate sensitivities — IFAM aluminum foams gained +18% in crush strength under impact while Cymat foams gained +0%, and iron hollow spheres showed +55–59% enhancement — indicating that relative rankings shift with loading rate (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 9-12). The four mechanisms responsible are entrapped-air pressure, base-material strain-rate sensitivity, shock-wave enhancement (significant above ~45 m/s impact velocity), and micro-inertia (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 12-14). Micro-inertia is particularly relevant: it can suppress compliant buckling modes in "type II" structures (sharp post-yield force drop), producing pronounced dynamic strengthening, while "type I" structures (flat post-yield plateau) show limited rate sensitivity (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17). Liu et al. (2009) confirmed that the overall rate effect of a honeycomb structure was much weaker than the rate sensitivity of the constituent cell-wall material and that different deformation modes emerge at different impact-velocity ranges (liu2009anumericalstudy pages 2-3, liu2009anumericalstudy pages 1-2).

**Implications for BEAR GCS designs.** The BEAR's best-performing PLA shells exhibit type-I behavior (long, flat post-yield plateaus exploiting progressive plastic buckling and self-contact) (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 4-7). Under impact, PLA is glassy and has limited strain-rate sensitivity compared to metals, so micro-inertia and shock effects would be the dominant rate-dependent mechanisms. Below ~45 m/s (the egg-drop regime for h ≤ ~100 m), shock enhancement is expected to be negligible (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 12-14). The flat-plateau (type I) character of the BEAR shells suggests their K_s ranking may be approximately preserved at low to moderate impact velocities, but this has not been experimentally validated. The 2024 paper's K_s metric (quasi-static compression efficiency) is not directly comparable to peak-g or h_crit in a free-fall drop without a conversion model that accounts for inertial effects, densification dynamics, and egg fragility thresholds.

## 3. Single-Use vs. Reusable

**The answer is material-dependent.** The 2024 campaign explicitly characterized rebound fraction (post-compression height recovery after one minute) and found a clear bifurcation between material classes (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 20-23):

- **Plastic polymers (PLA, PETG, Nylon):** The PLA "Willow" component was "permanently flattened to ~23% of its initial height" after compression (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 4-5). These are effectively **single-use, crushable energy absorbers** that undergo irreversible plastic deformation and densification — corresponding to category (a) "crushable foam/lattice cushion" from the prior follow-up task.

- **Hyperelastic polymers (TPU-2, TPE):** The TPU-2 component "recovers ~99% of its height one minute after compression" (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 4-5). These are **reusable, elastically recoverable cushions** — corresponding to category (b) "elastic recoverable cushion."

The seven materials tested were: TPE (Chinchilla/Ninjatek), TPU-1 (NinjaFlex/Ninjatek), TPU-2 (Cheetah/Ninjatek), TPU-3 (Armadillo/Ninjatek), Nylon (MatterHackers Pro Series), PETG (MatterHackers Pro Series), and PLA (eSun PLA+/MakerGear) (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26, snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8). The superlative K_s = 75.2% was achieved with PLA (a plastic, single-use material), while TPU-based designs achieved substantially lower K_s* ≈ 53% (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10). This means the record-setting BEAR structure is a **single-use crushable absorber**, not a reusable elastic cushion. The BEAR GCS is not a tensegrity (category e) — it is a continuous thin-walled shell, topologically and mechanically distinct from a cable-strut system.

**Assessment of the four sub-questions:**

**(i) Can the BEAR-discovered best unit cell be FFF-printed on a consumer printer?** **Yes.** The 2024 paper provides open-source STL-generation code at https://github.com/bu-shapelab/gcs (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8), documents all 11 geometric parameters and their ranges (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26), and reports printing settings (MakerGear M3, 0.5/0.75 mm nozzle, 15 mm/s vase-mode, standard temperatures) that are compatible with Bambu H2D-class hardware (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8). The experiment dataset is shared at kablab.org/data (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39). The authors demonstrated that the Willow design prints reproducibly across five printers (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39).

**(ii) Can it be used as a baseline curve on peak-g vs. drop height?** **Yes, with major caveats.** The BEAR's K_s is a quasi-static efficiency metric, not a peak-g measurement. To place a BEAR shell on a peak-g vs. h plot, one would need to either (a) experimentally drop-test the reprinted shell, or (b) develop an analytical/FEA model converting the known σ–ε curve to an impact-deceleration pulse. Simply plotting K_s alongside peak-g is apples-to-oranges.

**(iii) Can it be interpreted as a closed-loop-optimized baseline against which the tensegrity is compared?** **Yes, this framing is defensible** — the BEAR shell represents what an automated BO search converges to within a parametric cylindrical-shell design space, and the tensegrity is a topologically distinct class-1 cable-strut system outside that search space (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2). The comparison narrative is: "BEAR found the best shell; our BO finds the best tensegrity; how do they compare under the same drop test?"

**(iv) Technical issues:**
- **Reproducibility:** Strong — open-source code, documented parameters, consumer FFF compatible (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8).
- **FoM comparability:** **Apples-to-oranges** unless the BEAR shell is physically drop-tested under the benchmark protocol. K_s (quasi-static efficiency) ≠ peak-g (dynamic deceleration) (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 9-12, zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17).
- **Licensing:** No proprietary constraints identified; code is on GitHub, data are on kablab.org (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39).
- **"Superlative" claim under impact:** **Not validated.** The 75.2% K_s record was demonstrated only under quasi-static loading. Under impact, the ranking may be approximately preserved for type-I PLA shells at moderate velocities (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17), but this has not been experimentally confirmed.

**Recommendation: Yes-with-caveats.** Include the BEAR shell as a baseline only if it is physically drop-tested under the shared benchmark protocol. Do not extrapolate the K_s = 75.2% claim to impact performance without experimental validation.

## 5. Better Alternative Baselines if BEAR Is Not Appropriate

The closest published work combining ML/BO-guided design with impact testing is:

**Gu et al. (2016), *Extreme Mechanics Letters*.** This MIT study fabricated nacre-like brick-and-mortar polymer composites via multi-material 3D printing (Stratasys Connex 3) and tested them under drop-weight impact at ~2.3–4 m/s impact velocities (gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 2-3, gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 3-5). ## 2. Loading-Regime Applicability to a Drag-Free Egg Drop

**All published BEAR results were obtained under quasi-static compression.** The original 2020 study used 3 mm/min displacement on an Instron (gongora2020abayesianexperimental pages 5-6), and the 2024 campaign used 2 mm/min (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 13-16). For the sample heights tested (~20 mm), this corresponds to nominal strain rates of order 10⁻³ s⁻¹ — firmly in the quasi-static regime. No impact testing (drop-tower or otherwise) was reported in the retrievable papers, with the possible exception of the 2022 *Matter* paper whose full content was unavailable.

**Extrapolation to free-fall egg-drop impact is problematic.** A drag-free egg drop from, say, 5 m produces an impact velocity of approximately 10 m/s (ε̇ on the order of 10²–10³ s⁻¹ for a 20 mm cushion), representing a strain-rate increase of five to six orders of magnitude over the BEAR test conditions. The cellular-solids literature demonstrates that geometry rankings under quasi-static loading do not necessarily hold under dynamic impact. Zhao et al. (2005) showed that different cellular geometries exhibit markedly different rate sensitivities — IFAM aluminum foams gained +18% in crush strength under impact while Cymat foams gained +0%, and iron hollow spheres showed +55–59% enhancement — indicating that relative rankings shift with loading rate (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 9-12). The four mechanisms responsible are entrapped-air pressure, base-material strain-rate sensitivity, shock-wave enhancement (significant above ~45 m/s impact velocity), and micro-inertia (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 12-14). Micro-inertia is particularly relevant: it can suppress compliant buckling modes in "type II" structures (sharp post-yield force drop), producing pronounced dynamic strengthening, while "type I" structures (flat post-yield plateau) show limited rate sensitivity (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17). Liu et al. (2009) confirmed that the overall rate effect of a honeycomb structure was much weaker than the rate sensitivity of the constituent cell-wall material and that different deformation modes emerge at different impact-velocity ranges (liu2009anumericalstudy pages 2-3, liu2009anumericalstudy pages 1-2).

**Implications for BEAR GCS designs.** The BEAR's best-performing PLA shells exhibit type-I behavior (long, flat post-yield plateaus exploiting progressive plastic buckling and self-contact) (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 4-7). Under impact, PLA is glassy and has limited strain-rate sensitivity compared to metals, so micro-inertia and shock effects would be the dominant rate-dependent mechanisms. Below ~45 m/s (the egg-drop regime for h ≤ ~100 m), shock enhancement is expected to be negligible (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 12-14). The flat-plateau (type I) character of the BEAR shells suggests their K_s ranking may be approximately preserved at low to moderate impact velocities, but this has not been experimentally validated. The 2024 paper's K_s metric (quasi-static compression efficiency) is not directly comparable to peak-g or h_crit in a free-fall drop without a conversion model that accounts for inertial effects, densification dynamics, and egg fragility thresholds.

## 3. Single-Use vs. Reusable

**The answer is material-dependent.** The 2024 campaign explicitly characterized rebound fraction (post-compression height recovery after one minute) and found a clear bifurcation between material classes (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 20-23):

- **Plastic polymers (PLA, PETG, Nylon):** The PLA "Willow" component was "permanently flattened to ~23% of its initial height" after compression (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 4-5). These are effectively **single-use, crushable energy absorbers** that undergo irreversible plastic deformation and densification — corresponding to category (a) "crushable foam/lattice cushion" from the prior follow-up task.

- **Hyperelastic polymers (TPU-2, TPE):** The TPU-2 component "recovers ~99% of its height one minute after compression" (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 4-5). These are **reusable, elastically recoverable cushions** — corresponding to category (b) "elastic recoverable cushion."

The seven materials tested were: TPE (Chinchilla/Ninjatek), TPU-1 (NinjaFlex/Ninjatek), TPU-2 (Cheetah/Ninjatek), TPU-3 (Armadillo/Ninjatek), Nylon (MatterHackers Pro Series), PETG (MatterHackers Pro Series), and PLA (eSun PLA+/MakerGear) (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26, snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8). The superlative K_s = 75.2% was achieved with PLA (a plastic, single-use material), while TPU-based designs achieved substantially lower K_s* ≈ 53% (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 7-10). This means the record-setting BEAR structure is a **single-use crushable absorber**, not a reusable elastic cushion. The BEAR GCS is not a tensegrity (category e) — it is a continuous thin-walled shell, topologically and mechanically distinct from a cable-strut system.

**Assessment of the four sub-questions:**

**(i) Can the BEAR-discovered best unit cell be FFF-printed on a consumer printer?** **Yes.** The 2024 paper provides open-source STL-generation code at https://github.com/bu-shapelab/gcs (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8), documents all 11 geometric parameters and their ranges (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26), and reports printing settings (MakerGear M3, 0.5/0.75 mm nozzle, 15 mm/s vase-mode, standard temperatures) that are compatible with Bambu H2D-class hardware (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8). The experiment dataset is shared at kablab.org/data (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39). The authors demonstrated that the Willow design prints reproducibly across five printers (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39).

**(ii) Can it be used as a baseline curve on peak-g vs. drop height?** **Yes, with major caveats.** The BEAR's K_s is a quasi-static efficiency metric, not a peak-g measurement. To place a BEAR shell on a peak-g vs. h plot, one would need to either (a) experimentally drop-test the reprinted shell, or (b) develop an analytical/FEA model converting the known σ–ε curve to an impact-deceleration pulse. Simply plotting K_s alongside peak-g is apples-to-oranges.

**(iii) Can it be interpreted as a closed-loop-optimized baseline against which the tensegrity is compared?** **Yes, this framing is defensible** — the BEAR shell represents what an automated BO search converges to within a parametric cylindrical-shell design space, and the tensegrity is a topologically distinct class-1 cable-strut system outside that search space (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2). The comparison narrative is: "BEAR found the best shell; our BO finds the best tensegrity; how do they compare under the same drop test?"

**(iv) Technical issues:**
- **Reproducibility:** Strong — open-source code, documented parameters, consumer FFF compatible (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8).
- **FoM comparability:** **Apples-to-oranges** unless the BEAR shell is physically drop-tested under the benchmark protocol. K_s (quasi-static efficiency) ≠ peak-g (dynamic deceleration) (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 9-12, zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17).
- **Licensing:** No proprietary constraints identified; code is on GitHub, data are on kablab.org (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8, snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39).
- **"Superlative" claim under impact:** **Not validated.** The 75.2% K_s record was demonstrated only under quasi-static loading. Under impact, the ranking may be approximately preserved for type-I PLA shells at moderate velocities (zhao2005anexperimentalstudy pages 14-17), but this has not been experimentally confirmed.

**Recommendation: Yes-with-caveats.** Include the BEAR shell as a baseline only if it is physically drop-tested under the shared benchmark protocol. Do not extrapolate the K_s = 75.2% claim to impact performance without experimental validation.

## 5. Better Alternative Baselines if BEAR Is Not Appropriate

The closest published work combining ML/BO-guided design with impact testing is:

**Gu et al. (2016), *Extreme Mechanics Letters*.** This MIT study fabricated nacre-like brick-and-mortar polymer composites via multi-material 3D printing (Stratasys Connex 3) and tested them under drop-weight impact at ~2.3–4 m/s impact velocities (gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 2-3, gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 3-5). The nacre-like laminate arrested the impactor completely (residual velocity = 0 m/s) while the monolithic stiff material was perforated (residual velocity ~1 m/s) (gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 3-5, gu2016biomimeticadditivemanufactured pages 5-6). However, this study used proprietary Stratasys photopolymers (VeroMagenta/TangoBlackPlus) not reproducible on FFF printers, the optimization was FEA-guided rather than closed-loop BO, and the architecture (flat laminate panel) is not directly comparable to a space-filling egg-drop cushion.

**Gongora et al. (2022), *Matter*.** This Brown-lab paper — "Designing lattices for impact protection using transfer learning" — is the most promising alternative because it explicitly targets impact protection and applies transfer-learning methodology from the BEAR ecosystem. Its full details were not retrievable for this review, but it likely bridges the quasi-static-to-impact gap that limits the 2024 Nature Communications paper. If obtainable, this would be the strongest candidate for a "BO-optimized FFF-printed energy absorber under impact" baseline.

**Li et al. (2024), *Science Advances*.** This MIT/CSAIL study used a nested-loop computational discovery pipeline to find microstructured composites with optimal stiffness-toughness Pareto trade-offs, achieving up to 175.6% higher toughness than baselines (gu2018denovocomposite pages 11-13). However, the optimization target was quasi-static fracture toughness, not impact energy absorption.

No published work was found that combines all three elements — (1) fully autonomous closed-loop BO, (2) FFF-printed lattice/shell geometry, and (3) experimental impact-velocity testing — in a single study. This gap represents an open opportunity.

## 6. Concrete Recommendation

**Recommendation: Cite the BEAR as conceptually related prior art for the BO methodology, and use the BEAR "Willow" GCS shell as a physically drop-tested baseline entry only if re-fabricated and tested under the shared benchmark protocol.** Specifically, the BEAR K_s = 75.2% quasi-static record (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 1-2) should not be directly plotted on a peak-g vs. drop-height chart because the figures of merit are incommensurable without impact testing. Instead, the recommended approach is twofold: (a) reprint the BEAR "Willow" PLA shell (or its TPU-2 "Iroko" counterpart for a reusable comparison) using the open-source GitHub code (snapp2024superlativemechanicalenergy pages 7-8), physically drop-test it under the shared benchmark constraints (Ø 200 mm, m_sys ≤ 500 g, rigid ASTM D5276 floor), and plot the measured h_crit alongside the foam, honeycomb, and tensegrity entries; and (b) frame the project narrative as "BEAR for tensegrities" — applying Brown's autonomous Bayesian optimization methodology to the topologically distinct class-1 tensegrity design space — citing the BEAR papers as the inspiration and methodological template for the autonomous-optimization campaign rather than as a directly comparable impact-performance baseline. This framing is natural because the tensegrity is outside the BEAR's parametric GCS search space, the loading regimes differ (quasi-static crush vs. free-fall impact), and the best BEAR result (PLA, single-use) is in a fundamentally different reusability category than the elastic tensegrity. The Gongora et al. (2022) *Matter* paper on transfer learning for impact protection, if obtained in full, could strengthen the bridge between quasi-static BEAR records and impact-regime comparisons.
